file: papers/pdf/Mirvahedi and Morrish - 2017 - The Role of Serendipity in Opportunity Exploration.pdf
about: An empirical multiple-case study of fast-growth firms in New Zealand and Iran examining how serendipity contributes to opportunity exploration, identifying patterns (Archimedean, Columbian, Galilean and a new 'entrepreneurial serendipity') and sources such as networks, luck and perseverance.

candidates.label: Accident plus sagacity
candidates.definition: Serendipity is a combination of a lucky accident and the person's ability (sagacity, knowledge, deduction) to recognise and develop what was found; pure chance alone is not serendipity.
candidates.applies_when: An account describes an accidental encounter AND the person actively recognising its value or making use of it.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: The event is described as pure luck with no recognition or action by the person; the authors distinguish this as luck/chance rather than serendipity.

candidates.label: Archimedean serendipity
candidates.definition: Looking for a specified opportunity or solution and accidentally finding that same thing, typically with orderly search and high knowledge.
candidates.applies_when: The person was seeking a particular solution or opportunity and found it through a chance event (e.g., seeking consultants and meeting them through a chance encounter).
candidates.does_not_apply_when: What was found differs from what was sought (Columbian) or nothing specific was sought (Galilean/entrepreneurial).

candidates.label: Columbian serendipity
candidates.definition: Looking for one specified opportunity and finding a different one instead.
candidates.applies_when: The account shows search for a specific target that led to discovery of something else of value.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: The thing found is the thing sought (Archimedean).

candidates.label: Galilean serendipity
candidates.definition: Finding an unspecified opportunity one was not seeking at all, recognised through knowledge or sagacity; often at firm formation when the person had no intention or idea of business.
candidates.applies_when: Someone with no intention to start or pursue a business stumbles on an opportunity or receives an out-of-the-blue offer (e.g., offered a partnership, noticing a gap while shopping).
candidates.does_not_apply_when: The person was already wanting to start some business and waiting for any opportunity (entrepreneurial serendipity).

candidates.label: Entrepreneurial serendipity
candidates.definition: A new pattern where the person seeks any type of unspecified opportunity (e.g., to be self-employed) and through serendipitous circumstances finds an appropriate one; search may be orderly or haphazard and knowledge high or low; occurs continuously with a prepared mind.
candidates.applies_when: The person wanted to run their own business or expand without a particular idea and an opportunity came along that they seized.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: The person had no readiness or purpose to receive a business idea (Galilean).

candidates.label: Out-of-the-blue offer
candidates.definition: An unexpected invitation to join a business or partnership that starts the venture.
candidates.applies_when: Account reports being offered a partnership, job in a firm, or invitation that led to the venture without prior seeking.

candidates.label: Chance encounter or everyday experience
candidates.definition: Unplanned encounters (holiday meetings, university meetings, teaching a student) or everyday activities (buying a camera, visiting a website) that reveal an opportunity.
candidates.applies_when: An opportunity is reported as arising from a chance meeting or an incidental personal experience.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: The contact came through deliberate, systematic information search.

candidates.label: External environmental events
candidates.definition: Unexpected environmental events (earthquake, recession, a sporting event, competitors' problems) that bring big projects or expansion.
candidates.applies_when: A venture benefited from an unplanned external event or shift in the environment.

candidates.label: Recognising and seizing the moment
candidates.definition: Entrepreneurs must recognise the value of the chance event and respond quickly by leveraging resources to turn it into an opportunity.
candidates.applies_when: Account shows the person noticing value in an unexpected event and acting promptly on it.

candidates.label: Orderly versus haphazard search
candidates.definition: Search for opportunities ranges from organised, purposeful search to haphazard, unprepared finding without search criteria; serendipity patterns differ by search type.
candidates.applies_when: Account describes how the person was looking: deliberately trying things/looking, or not searching at all.

candidates.label: Activation of dormant knowledge
candidates.definition: Knowledge lying unused in the entrepreneur's mind becomes explicit through a contingency such as meeting a friend or visiting a website.
candidates.applies_when: An earlier, unused skill or qualification suddenly becomes relevant because of a chance event.

candidates.label: Personal and business networks
candidates.definition: Networks are the most frequent source of serendipity; personal networks especially early, business networks as firms grow; referrals through friends and family bring big projects.
candidates.applies_when: An opportunity arrives via a friend, spouse, colleague, referral or business contact.

candidates.label: Prior knowledge and prepared mind
candidates.definition: Serendipity requires a mind ready to capture something; prior knowledge and experience (high or low) shape which pattern occurs.
candidates.applies_when: Account links recognition of a chance opportunity to the person's existing knowledge, experience or readiness.

candidates.label: Knowledge, search and contingency
candidates.definition: Following Dew, serendipitous discovery draws on prior knowledge, search and contingency together.
candidates.applies_when: An account combines what the person knew, how they were searching, and a contingent event.

candidates.label: Perseverance and hard work
candidates.definition: Persistence and hard work are reported sources of serendipity; entrepreneurs say they create their own luck and hard work puts them in the right place.
candidates.applies_when: Entrepreneur links chance opportunities to persistence, not giving up, or working hard.

candidates.label: Quality products and serving clients
candidates.definition: Commitment to clients through high-quality products and services opens new windows of opportunity and is a source of serendipity.
candidates.applies_when: Chance opportunities are attributed to reputation for quality or service commitment.

candidates.label: Alertness and openness
candidates.definition: Entrepreneurial alertness and being alert to environmental changes lead entrepreneurs to treat options as opportunities; positive outlook believed to bring good things.
candidates.applies_when: Entrepreneur describes staying alert or open, or a mind-set ready to seize any opportunity.

candidates.label: Desire for self-employment
candidates.definition: Dissatisfaction with employment or boredom in a previous job creates readiness to seize any opportunity that comes along.
candidates.applies_when: Person reports disliking being an employee or wanting their own business before the opportunity appeared.

candidates.label: Early stage and scarce resources
candidates.definition: Serendipity is likely at early stages of firm formation, and obtaining ideas through serendipity is prevalent in resource-scarce firms; knowledge spill-over increases it.
candidates.applies_when: Serendipitous events cluster around founding or occur in resource-poor young firms.

candidates.label: Starting the venture
candidates.definition: Serendipity provides the initial business idea, first project or entry into the industry.
candidates.applies_when: Founding idea, first contract or entry into business arose serendipitously.

candidates.label: Advancing or redirecting the venture
candidates.definition: Serendipity after founding brings big orders, partners, new markets, changed business models or expansion; its significance was judged by changes of direction, great ideas or new markets.
candidates.applies_when: An established firm gains a new market, partner, big contract, or changes direction through a chance event.

candidates.label: New opportunities and growth
candidates.definition: Serendipity leads to new opportunities that entrepreneurs explore to achieve growth.
candidates.applies_when: Account links a serendipitous event to growth or major new opportunity.

candidates.label: Luck, chance, fate language
candidates.definition: Entrepreneurs talk about serendipity using luck, chance, fortune and fate interchangeably and see it as a business fact needed for success.
candidates.applies_when: Interviewee describes events using luck/chance/fate/fortune vocabulary.

candidates.label: Own role over luck
candidates.definition: Entrepreneurs see their own role as more salient than serendipity, yet concede it cannot be ignored; they claim to create their own luck.
candidates.applies_when: Interviewee downplays luck in favour of their effort while acknowledging chance.

candidates.label: Right opportunity at right time
candidates.definition: Entrepreneurs believe the right opportunity appears at the right time and wait for it.
candidates.applies_when: Interviewee narrates waiting for the right moment or that things came when the time was right.

candidates.label: Pure luck or chance
candidates.definition: Events attributed to pure luck without sagacity, or finding a specified opportunity via haphazard search with little knowledge, are luck rather than serendipity.
candidates.applies_when: An outcome explained solely by chance, with no recognition or knowledge-based action, or a dream realised by lucky haphazard search.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: The person's sagacity or action in recognising/exploiting the accident is evident (serendipity).

candidates.label: Deliberate search and planning
candidates.definition: Opportunities can arise from deliberate, goal-oriented search, market research, information asymmetries or planned strategy, contrasted with serendipitous encounters.
candidates.applies_when: Opportunity is attributed to systematic research, planned strategy or problem-solution search.
